title: Hamming Distance
description: Brute force to optimized: checking all 32 positions versus XOR combined with bit clearing.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given two integers x and y, return the Hamming distance between them, the number of bit positions at which their binary representations differ.

blocks.caption: Input flows through XOR-then-count-set-bits to produce the Hamming distance

blocks.text: Given two integers x and y, return the Hamming distance between them, the number of positions at which their binary representations differ.

blocks.title: Analogy: Counting Mismatched Switches Between Two Panels
blocks.text: Like comparing two rows of on-off switches side by side and counting exactly how many positions have a switch flipped differently between the two rows.

blocks.caption: XOR reveals every position where the two numbers differ, then those positions are counted

blocks.text: If both numbers are identical, every bit position matches exactly, so the Hamming distance is 0.
Before jumping into a bit by bit comparison, it helps to notice what operation naturally highlights differences between two binary numbers.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Comparing x and y bit by bit means checking, for every position, whether the two bits are the same or different.

Observation 2: XOR is defined exactly as "1 where the two bits differ, 0 where they match", and it performs this comparison for all bit positions in a single operation, not one at a time.

Observation 3: Once XOR has revealed every differing position as a 1 bit, the Hamming distance is simply the number of 1 bits set in that XOR result.

Observation 4: Counting set bits is itself a well known subproblem, so this becomes two familiar operations chained together rather than one new algorithm.

So the real question isn't 'how do I compare two numbers bit by bit', it's 'how do I count the set bits in x XOR y', a problem you may already know how to solve efficiently.
Keep this XOR then count framing in mind while working through the brute force solution below, since it's exactly the shortcut the optimized solution uses.
Check every one of the 32 bit positions individually, extracting the corresponding bit from both x and y, and counting how many positions disagree.

items: For each of the 32 bit positions, extract that bit from both x and y using shifting and masking.
If the two extracted bits differ, increment the count.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The loop always runs exactly 32 times regardless of x and y, because a fixed width integer always has 32 bit positions to check, even if most of them already match.
Shifting each number right by i and masking with 1 isolates exactly one bit at a time, which is the most direct way to inspect an individual bit position.
The count only increases when the two extracted bits differ, directly mirroring the problem's definition of Hamming distance.

blocks.text: Every bit position of both numbers is directly compared, so every differing position is correctly counted.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(32), a fixed number of comparisons.
Space: O(1), only a counter is kept.
Limitation: extracting and comparing each bit of both numbers separately does more work than necessary, when a single XOR operation could reveal every differing position at once.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why brute force is limited: it inspects all 32 positions even when most of them already match, wasting work on positions that agree.

What it wastes: time spent extracting and comparing bits that are identical in x and y contributes nothing to the final answer.

Can we avoid the wasted work: yes. XOR the two numbers once, and every differing position becomes a 1 automatically, with no manual per bit comparison needed.

Can the results combine into one step: yes. After XOR, the problem becomes identical to "count the set bits in a single number", solvable with Brian Kernighan's technique in a number of steps equal to only the differing bits, not all 32.

XOR x and y together: every bit position where they differ becomes a 1 in the result, and every position where they match becomes a 0. The Hamming distance is then simply the number of set bits in this XOR result, which can be counted efficiently using Brian Kernighan's bit clearing technique instead of checking all 32 positions.
XOR the two numbers, then count the set bits in the result using repeated bit clearing.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["x XOR y","001 XOR 100 = 101","XOR marks every bit position where x and y disagree with a 1"],["Clear the lowest set bit of 101","101 AND 100 = 100, count = 1","x AND (x-1) always clears exactly the lowest set bit, letting us count that bit and move on"],["Clear the lowest set bit of 100","100 AND 011 = 000, count = 2","The second and final set bit is cleared the same way, bringing the result to zero"],["Result reaches 0, stop","answer is 2","Once no bits remain set, every differing position has been counted"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized: XOR reveals differing bits at once, then count them with bit clearing

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(number of differing bits), since the loop runs only as many times as there are set bits in the XOR result.
Space: O(1), only a counter and the XOR result are kept.

XOR is a bitwise operation that is 1 exactly when the two input bits differ, so applying it once to the entire numbers produces a result whose set bits are precisely the differing positions between x and y. Counting those set bits therefore counts exactly the Hamming distance, with no risk of missing or double counting a position.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Bit of x","Bit of y","XOR Result","Counted as Differing?"],"rows":[["0","0","0","No, bits match"],["0","1","1","Yes, bits differ"],["1","0","1","Yes, bits differ"],["1","1","0","No, bits match"]]}

items: xorResult = x ^ y computes every differing bit position in one operation, replacing the need to inspect each of the 32 positions individually.
The while loop only runs as many times as there are set bits remaining in xorResult, so it does no extra work for positions that already matched.
xorResult &= (xorResult - 1) is Brian Kernighan's trick: subtracting 1 flips the lowest set bit and everything below it, and ANDing with the original clears exactly that lowest set bit.

blocks.text: This problem combines two foundational bit manipulation ideas directly: XOR to reveal differences between two values, and Brian Kernighan's bit clearing to count set bits efficiently, both of which reappear constantly across bit manipulation problems.

items: Comparing x and y bit by bit manually instead of recognizing that a single XOR operation already reveals every differing position at once, which adds unnecessary code and obscures the real insight.
Using a fixed 32 iteration loop to count the XOR result's set bits instead of the faster bit clearing technique, which does extra work on bit positions that are already zero.
Forgetting that XOR is symmetric, since x XOR y equals y XOR x, leading to unnecessary special casing of argument order that is not actually needed.

blocks.text: Point out explicitly that this problem is really "Number of 1 Bits" applied to the XOR of two numbers, connecting it directly to that more foundational problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If they say "can you avoid checking every bit position", think XOR, since it identifies all differences in one operation.
If they say "can you count the set bits faster", think Brian Kernighan's bit clearing, which only loops as many times as there are set bits.
If they ask "does this remind you of another problem", think Number of 1 Bits, since this problem is that one applied to x XOR y.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(32) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (XOR plus bit clearing): O(number of differing bits) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: XOR to reveal bit differences, then count set bits
Core Idea: x XOR y turns every differing bit position into a 1, reducing the problem to counting set bits
Time: O(number of differing bits) with bit clearing, O(32) with brute force
Space: O(1) in both approaches
Most Important Observation: comparing two numbers bit by bit is the same as counting the set bits in their XOR
Interview Difficulty: Beginner, a great warm-up for XOR based bit manipulation problems
One-line memory trick: Hamming distance is just 'Number of 1 Bits' in disguise, applied to x XOR y
